world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Santandrea, Stefano 1961. Comparative Outline-Grammar of Ndogo-Sere-Tagbu-Bai-Bviri. Bologna. Not found online.

new_statements.quote: p.15: "4. ACCENT In order to obtain a good pronunciation of these languages, especially of Ndogo, great attention must be paid to the accent. The following suggestions (I shall not call them rules) may serve as a [guide for Ndogo]. [...] III. The most noteworthy difference in accent exists among words of two syllables, some having an even stress on both syllables, and some having a real accent on the first." p.29: "(d) As hinted above (5. iv.), the accent usually lies on the first syllable of dissyllables: thus, in reduplication, accents lie on the first and third syllables. Out of the numerous examples given above only mbulàmbulà makes an exception"
new_statements.citation: Santandrea, Stefano. 1961. Comparative Outline-Grammar of Ndogo-Sere-Tagbu-Bai-Bviri. (Museum Combonianum 13.) Bologna: Editrice Nigrizia.
new_statements.locator: Introductory Notes, sec. 4 'ACCENT', p. 15 (opening and remark III); sec. 5 'TONE', point (d), p. 29
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.rule_in_words: Group-level rule for the Ndogo-Sere-Tagbu-Bai-Bviri languages with Ndogo as the model: monosyllables carry their accent trivially; compound polysyllables keep an accent on each component; dissyllables either have even stress on both syllables or a real accent on the first syllable (the latter typically when the second syllable has l, r or n, and that syllable is often lost); the accent 'usually lies on the first syllable of dissyllables'; reduplicated dissyllables accent syllables 1 and 3. The languages are tonal (four levels: low, mid, high, very high), so accent is described alongside tone.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed as such; compounds have an accent on each component and reduplications have accents on the first and third syllables.
new_statements.exceptions: Dissyllables with 'even stress on both syllables'; reduplicated mbulambula (accent on the second syllable of each component); Bviri final-vowel loss (remark V).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (citation forms of nouns/verbs). CAVEAT: the accent section is explicitly 'a guide for Ndogo' and is extended by name only to Bviri (remark V); Tagbu is not named on the page (HTRC token list for p. 15 has no Sere/Tagbu token) and Santandrea 1948 says Tagbu phonetics is closer to Sere than to Ndogo. Only Google Books snippets and HathiTrust page tokens were available, not the full page.
new_statements.identity_note: Santandrea's Tagbu are the c. 100 speakers resettled at Ngua near Mboro/Bisellia (Wau area, South Sudan), whose language 'stands between Ndogo and Sere, resembling closely the former in vocabulary, but more closely the latter in phonetics' (Santandrea 1948) and of which Santandrea 1961 p. 103 says 'There is great resemblance between Sere and Tagbu'; Tucker & Bryan 1956 suggest they 'may be the same as' the Basiri/Sere. Ethnologue and Wikipedia place tbm 'Tagbo (Tagbu, Tagba)' in DR Congo (17,000 speakers), and Santandrea 1964 has 'no reliable information' about the 'Belgian Congo Tagbu'; Glottolog tagb1255 (countries SS) covers both. The quoted accent statement is a group-level rule modelled on Ndogo (ndog1248) and extended by name only to Bviri (bela1255); Tagbu is not named in it.
